title: Microeconomics read-only wording and graph-assessment audit

method.text_screen: Every current Micro stem and choice was included in full-bank grammar, phrase, and repeated-family screening; candidate wording was then reviewed in context. This is not a new line-by-line answer-key or difficulty certification.
method.graph_review: All 1,195 image-bearing stems and option sets were reviewed with the image and equivalent accessibility description mentally hidden. All 233 referenced image files were visually inspected; five are byte-identical copies, leaving 228 distinct image contents.
method.scope: Canonical Composer Micro course-area membership resolved through the normal exporter read-only collection, answer-resolution and partition functions. No polished-game source banks were added.
method.shared_general: All shared records were included in screening. No style finding or approved General wording/graph revision was reopened. Two concrete residual shortcuts affect shared records absent from both completed change lists.
method.repair_status: Directions only, not replacement questions. The proposed construct and graph tests are acceptance criteria for later implementation, not claims that unwritten revisions have passed validation.

preservation_checks.reason_tests_not_run: Read-only content audit; no implementation or export regeneration requested. Read-only inventory and artifact-integrity checks were performed.

wording_findings.current_wording: A student claims that “TP is maximized where MP is maximized. / A learner says, “If the owner did not write a check, the resource has no cost.
wording_findings.why: Each stem ends inside an unclosed quotation and never asks the student to evaluate or correct the assertion. The total-product item also refers to a curve with no attached image.
wording_findings.direction: Close the quotation and add a direct request for the correct explanation. In B1-019, remove the orphan figure reference while preserving the conceptual TP/MP task; do not add an asset.

wording_findings.current_wording: Refer to the graph.
wording_findings.why: Neither canonical record has an image. The remaining text supplies the economic relationship, so the reference sends students looking for missing material.
wording_findings.direction: Remove the absent-graph reference and ask the existing conceptual relationship directly; preserve the present text-only task.

wording_findings.current_wording: price elasticity of demand generally: / Increase / Decline / Remain constant / Switch immediately from zero to infinity
wording_findings.why: The singular subject does not agree with any option’s verb.
wording_findings.direction: Use parallel singular verb forms, or turn the stem into a complete question; retain the elasticity distinction. Coordinate with its graph finding.

wording_findings.current_wording: Consumer surplus is $176 because add the demand triangle to all payments.
wording_findings.why: The distractor has a broken subordinate clause. Incorrect economic reasoning should still be grammatical.
wording_findings.direction: Express the intended mistaken addition in a complete clause. Coordinate with the graph revision; do not make the distractor economically correct.

wording_findings.current_wording: which cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium? / which pure-strategy Nash equilibrium follows?
wording_findings.why: The first two keyed answers contain two equilibria, and H-018 has none. Singular wording presupposes an answer structure the current alternatives do not provide.
wording_findings.direction: Ask for all pure-strategy Nash equilibria, if any; retain checking both firms’ unilateral deviations.

wording_findings.current_wording: assess whether the incumbent’s threatened response is credible / the alternative threat is credible
wording_findings.why: The stem does not identify the threatened action, and “alternative threat” has no clear antecedent. In fight outcomes the word alternative is especially confusing.
wording_findings.direction: Explicitly identify the incumbent’s threat to fight after entry and name that action in the alternatives. Preserve backward induction, including cases where a credible threat does not deter entry.

wording_findings.current_wording: A 1-unit allocation uses the cheapest 1 sellers ... among the highest 1 values.
wording_findings.why: The generated singular-number case retains plural nouns and an unnecessarily opaque recipient description.
wording_findings.direction: Use singular seller and identify the excluded highest-value buyer directly, retaining the $27 administrative resource cost and the existing allocation.

wording_findings.current_wording: The demand curve has different slopes in the two intervals over the shown interval
wording_findings.why: The ending repeats “interval” and contradicts the already plural comparison grammatically.
wording_findings.direction: Remove the redundant ending; retain the intended slope-versus-elasticity misconception in the distractor.

wording_findings.current_wording: Economic profit? / MP? / TC? / AFC?
wording_findings.why: These prompts read like worksheet notes. The surrounding data are often also compressed into comma-separated abbreviations.
wording_findings.direction: Ask a short complete question naming the requested economic quantity. Keep conventional abbreviations where established, all units, time periods, opportunity costs and numerical assumptions.

wording_findings.current_wording: Best correction? / Correction?
wording_findings.why: The detached label sounds like an authoring note rather than a direct question.
wording_findings.direction: Ask which statement corrects the specific misunderstanding; do not alter the repair role or underlying concept.

wording_findings.current_wording: In hypothetical consumer-choice case A, ...
wording_findings.why: Ninety-nine stems carry serial case-letter boilerplate that contributes no economic information and makes independent questions sound generated.
wording_findings.direction: Start with the consumer, prices, income or preferences. Remove only the case-label introduction; keep every condition and the intended consumer-choice reasoning.

wording_findings.current_wording: what is the new competitive-market direction?
wording_findings.why: “Market direction” does not name the outcomes being compared.
wording_findings.direction: Ask how the equilibrium wage and employment change, preserving the stated labor-demand assumption.

wording_findings.current_wording: Trace the effect into the related factor market.
wording_findings.why: The stock instruction is vague about the related input and the outcome to predict.
wording_findings.direction: Name the relevant complementary or substitute input and ask how its demand changes; retain cases where multiple input markets move differently.

wording_findings.current_wording: Which combined curve-and-decision result is correct?
wording_findings.why: This describes the assessment’s component skills using an invented compound phrase.
wording_findings.direction: Ask how the stated change affects cost curves and the firm’s short-run output decision. Preserve unavoidable fixed cost versus marginal-cost distinctions.

wording_findings.current_wording: What is the best integrated conclusion?
wording_findings.why: The closing describes integration rather than naming the economic result sought.
wording_findings.direction: Ask for the output decision and resulting economic profit or loss, retaining block sizes and the fixed-cost assumptions.

wording_findings.current_wording: Which output-profit decision is correct?
wording_findings.why: The compressed compound label is less natural than naming output and profit separately.
wording_findings.direction: Ask which output the firm should choose and what profit or loss results; preserve tie-breaking and current-versus-future avoidability.

wording_findings.current_wording: Which paired result is correct?
wording_findings.why: The stem never names the pair before students inspect the options.
wording_findings.direction: Ask for the profit-maximizing monopoly quantity and price; preserve demand and cost equations.

wording_findings.current_wording: Which comparison controls shutdown?
wording_findings.why: “Controls shutdown” is an awkward way to state the operating criterion.
wording_findings.direction: Ask which price-cost comparison determines whether the firm should continue producing in the short run.

wording_findings.current_wording: two crossings in this cost family / preserves allocative logic but removes profit
wording_findings.why: “Cost family” and “allocative logic” obscure standard cost-curve relationships and allocative efficiency.
wording_findings.direction: Name MC crossing AVC/ATC, or maintaining allocative efficiency while entry eliminates economic profit, as appropriate. Preserve the distinctions rather than substituting informal synonyms.

wording_findings.current_wording: Separate the unrealized gains into geometry and economic meaning.
wording_findings.why: This sounds like an instruction to the assessment author.
wording_findings.direction: Ask for the forgone total surplus and why those trades would have created gains. Retain the value-versus-cost interpretation alongside the area calculation.

wording_findings.current_wording: supports the social-intersection quantity / Which fiscal and price account
wording_findings.why: The noun phrases obscure an ordinary question about the efficient quantity, subsidy spending and buyer/seller prices.
wording_findings.direction: Name the socially efficient quantity and ask for government spending and the resulting buyer and seller prices. Coordinate with any later graph work.

wording_findings.current_wording: a ... policy in the opposite direction
wording_findings.why: The distractor describes an unspecified direction instead of naming the economic instrument.
wording_findings.direction: Name the intended opposite instrument (tax or subsidy), with the same unit and amount; preserve its intended error.

wording_findings.current_wording: Which channel creates the externality? / production or consumption channel
wording_findings.why: “Channel” adds abstraction where the distinction is simply whether production or consumption creates the spillover.
wording_findings.direction: Ask which activity creates the external cost or benefit, preserving the production/consumption distinction.

wording_findings.current_wording: what zero-profit geometry characterizes the standard long-run equilibrium?
wording_findings.why: “Zero-profit geometry” is assessment shorthand.
wording_findings.direction: Ask how demand and ATC relate in long-run equilibrium, retaining tangency rather than reducing the task to P=ATC alone.

wording_findings.current_wording: what vertical price–ATC gap represents profit on each unit? / The blue ATC guide ... lands on which dollar value? / The green AVC marker ... gives what variable cost per unit?
wording_findings.why: The stems narrate visual marks and geometry more than the economic quantity.
wording_findings.direction: Ask directly for profit per unit, average total cost or average variable cost at the specified output. Keep the graph necessary and retain the original introductory skill; do not remove useful graph labels.

wording_findings.current_wording: ... for the displayed firm
wording_findings.why: This repeated trailing phrase adds no information and sometimes follows a statement already about “the representative firm.” It reads like template padding.
wording_findings.direction: Remove the redundant tail and keep each alternative a complete, parallel economic statement. For graph targets, coordinate with stronger distractors rather than polishing obsolete options.

wording_findings.current_wording: the lowest-value buyer instead of the marginal buyer among the highest ... values
wording_findings.why: The nested ranking description forces students to decode wording before comparing willingness to pay.
wording_findings.direction: Identify the recipient and the excluded buyer by rank or value, preserving the efficient-allocation comparison, fixed output and any administrative resource cost.

wording_findings.current_wording: Which inference is safest? / Which welfare conclusion ... is safest?
wording_findings.why: “Safest” is understandable, but a direct statement about what the evidence supports is more typical instructor prose. This is preference, not a defect.
wording_findings.direction: Ask what conclusion is supported or what cannot be determined; keep uncertainty, causal limits and the revenue-versus-profit distinction.

wording_findings.current_wording: which statement is exact? / What is the exact error and correct result?
wording_findings.why: The word “exact” adds little to an ordinary selection or error-correction question. Precision itself remains legitimate where numerical rounding matters.
wording_findings.direction: Ask what changes or which correction is appropriate. Retain “exact” in instructions where it genuinely specifies how rounded inputs are to be treated.

wording_findings.current_wording: Checkpoint:
wording_findings.why: This labels the assessment stage inside the student-facing stem. It is harmless but unnecessary when the interface already identifies the stage.
wording_findings.direction: Remove the prefix if preferred while preserving all checkpoint metadata, difficulty and role.

wording_findings.current_wording: has chosen output Q1=...
wording_findings.why: The quantity is the long-run optimizing output; “chosen” is less precise but not incorrect.
wording_findings.direction: Use “profit-maximizing output” for this specific family, keeping efficient scale separate. Do not globally replace “chosen output” where the task is simply evaluating a stated quantity.

wording_findings.current_wording: Which statement about the Row firm’s dominant strategy is correct? / A / B
wording_findings.why: The stem asks for a statement while most choices are bare strategy names.
wording_findings.direction: Ask which strategy, if any, is strictly dominant; make alternatives parallel without changing dominance or best-response reasoning.

graph_findings.construct: Allocative efficiency as marginal willingness to pay equaling marginal cost
graph_findings.why: The question already calls the equilibrium or specified quantity efficient. The standard efficiency condition supplies the answer; equal surplus shares, fairness, or positive surplus for everyone do not.
graph_findings.repair: Require comparison of demand and supply values at a plotted alternative quantity with E, then select whether expansion or contraction recovers gains from trade. Offer two plausible value/cost comparisons, plus the actual values with the wrong efficiency conclusion.

graph_findings.construct: Total surplus versus payments, and forgone gains from underproduction
graph_findings.why: The stem gives the demand and supply intercepts, equilibrium coordinates and relevant quantity restriction. All required areas can be computed without the image.
graph_findings.repair: Leave at least one required intercept or marginal value/cost to the graph. Retain the revenue double-counting diagnosis or the efficiency loss from missing trades, pairing correct graph amounts with competing economic interpretations.

graph_findings.construct: Distinguishing consumer surplus, producer surplus, expenditure and total gains; efficiency versus distribution
graph_findings.why: Only the keyed option uses the correct welfare definition or separates efficiency from equal surplus shares. The wrong alternatives identify another economic quantity, count only one side, double count regions, require equal surplus, or misinterpret price times quantity. Its numerical claim need never be verified.
graph_findings.repair: Keep two alternatives using the correct economic definition but different graph-derived amounts or areas; include another using the correct amount with an incorrect interpretation. Preserve the named surplus or efficiency/distribution diagnosis.

graph_findings.construct: Zero producer surplus with constant marginal cost
graph_findings.why: The stem gives zero producer surplus despite positive revenue. Price equaling marginal cost on each unit is the sole economic explanation; no plotted observation is needed.
graph_findings.repair: Ask students to identify the plotted equilibrium price and producer surplus and explain why revenue is not producer surplus, without stating that surplus is zero.

graph_findings.construct: Surplus division under horizontal supply
graph_findings.why: The stem names horizontal supply at competitive equilibrium. Producer surplus is zero; only B states that, while the others equate revenue with surplus or add expenditure. The $72 figure does not discriminate.
graph_findings.repair: Retain two zero-producer-surplus alternatives with different graph-derived consumer-surplus amounts, plus the actual amount misclassified as revenue or producer surplus.

graph_findings.construct: Marginal gains and losses from underproduction and overproduction
graph_findings.why: The stem explicitly identifies output as below or above competitive equilibrium and labels it underproduction or overproduction. The appropriate marginal value/cost inequality follows without the graph.
graph_findings.repair: Remove the interpretation from the stem; require the plotted marginal value and cost at the specified output and the resulting recommendation to expand or contract.

graph_findings.construct: Efficiency losses versus transfers
graph_findings.why: Only the key treats missing beneficial trades or excess costly production as a total-surplus loss, or treats the stated transfer as distribution rather than a net welfare change. Other choices describe transfers or expenditure as welfare losses. The correct dollar amount is not checked.
graph_findings.repair: Offer two economically correct loss/recovery descriptions with different measured welfare areas; retain one correct area with the wrong transfer/efficiency interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Change in surplus on existing and additional trades
graph_findings.why: Only the key includes both changes on original trades and surplus on newly traded units. The other options explicitly count only one part, confuse expenditure with surplus, or confuse a level with a change.
graph_findings.repair: Keep two full-change calculations with different graph readings, and use the actual total with an incorrect attribution of its components.

graph_findings.construct: Budget feasibility, income and relative-price effects, and revealed normal/inferior-good responses
graph_findings.why: Every price, income, bundle and subsequent change needed for the task is stated in the stem. Budget arithmetic and the relevant economic relationship fully determine the answer without either image or accessibility description.
graph_findings.repair: Retain the subsequent hypothetical change but require original prices, an original intercept, or the relevant initial bundle to be inferred from the figure. Keep feasibility plus pivot/shift, relative-price interpretation, or normal/inferior classification in the alternatives; do not replace these with coordinate questions.

graph_findings.construct: Identifying the cause of a budget pivot or parallel shift
graph_findings.why: The stem names the outward pivot, inward pivot, or parallel inward shift. Only the key offers a price or income change consistent with that named transformation; the other changes have the wrong direction or shape, or concern preferences.
graph_findings.repair: Use at least two changes that produce the stated general transformation but different plotted intercepts or magnitudes; include an interpretation error at the observed intercepts.

graph_findings.construct: Unchanged budget intercepts and relative prices
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies a cereal-price change, an unchanged cereal intercept, or parallel budget lines. The general budget relationship identifies the unchanged intercept or price ratio; the numerical label on the correct choice is unnecessary.
graph_findings.repair: Require identification of the actual unchanged plotted intercept and an inference about which price or income changed, with multiple economically possible intercept/magnitude combinations.

graph_findings.construct: Indifference, ordinal utility, diminishing MRS, consistency, tangency and affordability
graph_findings.why: The question states the defining feature being tested (same indifference curve, convexity, an interior optimum/tangency, or a general affordability condition). A textbook definition answers it without any particular figure.
graph_findings.repair: Apply the same principle to plotted bundles, slopes or attainable curves whose relationships are not stated. Pair graph-specific evidence with an economic ranking or optimality conclusion, preserving the particular definition or reasoning skill.

graph_findings.construct: Utility maximization subject to a budget
graph_findings.why: Given affordable boundary points, only the key invokes a higher attainable indifference curve. Negative quantities, equal prices, zero spending, or incompleteness do not explain optimality. No comparison in the actual figure is needed.
graph_findings.repair: Require a comparison of two plausible affordable bundles and their attained curves; include the actual bundle with an incorrect justification such as merely exhausting the budget.

graph_findings.construct: Cash versus restricted vouchers and equimarginal adjustment after a price change
graph_findings.why: The stem explicitly supplies which utility level each policy can reach, or the initial marginal-utility-per-dollar equality and price change. The entire economic inference is textual.
graph_findings.repair: For the voucher item use the plotted attainable utility level as required evidence while preserving the policy comparison; for price adjustment require the graph-derived price ratio/tangency and compare it with the changed marginal condition.

graph_findings.construct: Marginal-average cost relationships
graph_findings.why: The stem locates output between the AVC and AC minima, or immediately right of the AC minimum. The standard marginal-average rule determines the correct ordering or rising-average explanation without the figure.
graph_findings.repair: Name only a plotted quantity, without its relationship to the minima. Require observed MC/AVC/AC values or positions plus the correct explanation of whether the averages rise or fall.

graph_findings.construct: Total cost equals fixed plus variable cost
graph_findings.why: The question asks the generic meaning of the TC–TVC difference or describes its constancy. TFC follows from the identity without any plotted magnitude.
graph_findings.repair: Use the plotted separation at a specified output to infer TFC and explain why it remains fixed as output changes. Offer two TFC amounts and the true amount misinterpreted as a marginal or average cost.

graph_findings.construct: Diminishing versus negative marginal product and marginal-average product relationships
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies the relevant position relative to a maximum, the sign of MP, the MP/AP comparison, or the rising-but-flattening TP shape. The requested consequence is the general marginal-total-average relationship.
graph_findings.repair: Give only a labor input or labeled interval and require its graph-derived MP/AP/TP evidence. Pair that evidence with the correct conclusion about total versus average output; retain competing interpretations of the same readings.

graph_findings.construct: Fixed cost per unit and marginal-average cost relationships
graph_findings.why: The stem gives the narrowing ATC–AVC separation or the MC/average-cost ordering, or asks the standard rule for an MC crossing. No graph-specific quantity or value is needed.
graph_findings.repair: Require actual cost readings or the labeled output where the relation holds, together with the economic implication for AFC or the direction of average cost. Do not supply the ordering to be inferred.

graph_findings.construct: Scale economies, minimum efficient scale and least-cost plant choice
graph_findings.why: The stem states the falling/flat/rising LRAC sequence, the first minimum-plateau point, or the complete ranking of plant costs. The key follows from the definition or least-cost rule.
graph_findings.repair: Require the plotted interval, threshold or cost of each feasible plant, then apply the scale-economy or least-cost interpretation. Include the same numerical evidence with a mistaken short-run/long-run inference.

graph_findings.construct: Minimum efficient scale
graph_findings.why: Only minimum efficient scale is a long-run average-cost concept. Marginal product, short-run shutdown and total revenue are not identified by an LRATC graph, so 60 need not be located.
graph_findings.repair: Offer two plausible output levels classified as minimum efficient scale, and the actual output with an incorrect interpretation. Keep the long-run cost-minimum concept necessary.

graph_findings.construct: Inverse relationship between productivity and marginal cost
graph_findings.why: Productivity improvement is supplied; only MP rising while MC falls is the standard implication with input prices fixed. The cost shift is not used.
graph_findings.repair: Require the observed before/after cost at a plotted output and infer the productivity effect, preserving the input-price assumption and the inverse MP/MC explanation.

graph_findings.construct: Elasticity versus slope, changing percentage bases, and revenue maximization
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies movement down a linear demand curve, constant slope with changing elasticity, or the revenue-maximizing point. The keyed answer is the standard rule rather than a graph-specific classification or value.
graph_findings.repair: Require elasticity or revenue evidence for actual labeled intervals, and a reason based on percentage changes rather than slope. For the revenue maximum, require identification of the plotted optimum plus its elasticity interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Elasticity and the total-revenue maximum on linear demand
graph_findings.why: The other alternatives contradict the revenue pattern on a downward-sloping linear demand curve, confuse constant slope with constant revenue, or assert zero revenue at its midpoint. Only the key gives a theoretically coherent pattern.
graph_findings.repair: Offer two coherent revenue sequences attached to different labeled points or magnitudes; include the observed sequence with a mistaken elasticity explanation.

graph_findings.construct: Perfectly inelastic demand
graph_findings.why: The stem calls D2 vertical. Only the key leaves quantity unchanged; the 50-unit reading can be ignored.
graph_findings.repair: Retain two unchanged-quantity alternatives with different graph values and one option using 50 with an incorrect elasticity classification.

graph_findings.construct: Time to adjust and supply elasticity
graph_findings.why: The stem gives the larger long-run response or identical starting point and price change; the usual time-horizon explanation or percentage-response identity supplies the answer.
graph_findings.repair: Require the two observed quantity responses or elasticities, then explain how adjustment opportunities account for their difference. Keep two economically plausible magnitudes and one correct pair with a wrong interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Revenue maximization subject to capacity
graph_findings.why: A explicitly sells 90 units despite capacity 70; B asserts a larger price cut guarantees revenue growth; C says capacity makes a price infeasible. Only D correctly applies the sales constraint, so its revenue figures need not be checked.
graph_findings.repair: Provide at least two capacity-respecting revenue comparisons for the candidate prices, then distinguish the correct graph-derived revenue pair and interpretation of binding capacity.

graph_findings.construct: Labor-market adjustment, derived demand, marginal efficiency, payroll measurement and combined shifts
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies all required wages/employment, productivity and output-price changes, shift directions or marginal-value/cost comparison. Theory and the stated numbers determine the answer without the graph.
graph_findings.repair: Keep the scenario or second change, but obtain the initial equilibrium, scale, demand direction or marginal comparison from the figure. Require the original economic diagnosis as well as the resulting graph-based magnitude or endpoint.

graph_findings.construct: Labor demand/supply shifts versus movements, equilibrium adjustment, binding floors and monopsony
graph_findings.why: The stem states the determinant, shift direction, binding control, curve intersection, or monopsony comparison, while the answers ask only the standard economic consequence. No plotted wage, employment or specific endpoint distinguishes the key.
graph_findings.repair: Retain the economic rule but require a plotted wage/employment change or a specific pair of intersections. Offer multiple economically coherent outcomes at different graph values, plus a correct-value interpretation error.

graph_findings.construct: Competitive wages, movement along supply, binding controls and monopsony hiring/wages
graph_findings.why: Only the key names the appropriate economic payment, unchanged-curve evidence, binding/nonbinding condition, labor-supply wage rule, or MFC=MRP hiring rule. Other options invoke irrelevant intercepts, curve shifts, zero scarcity or a wrong optimization condition; numerical evidence is not needed.
graph_findings.repair: Give two options satisfying the correct economic rule at different plotted wages or employment levels, and another using the actual values with the wrong rule. Preserve the competitive or monopsony distinction.

graph_findings.construct: Imports as excess demand and exports as excess supply
graph_findings.why: The stem already names the trade direction and gap. Only the key subtracts the correct domestic quantities in the appropriate order; the others reverse the gap, use autarky quantity, or multiply price and quantity.
graph_findings.repair: Give two directionally correct excess-demand/excess-supply calculations with different plotted quantities, plus the actual quantities with an incorrect trade interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Monopsony employment restriction and gains from additional hiring
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies both intersections, wages, MFC and MRP. The gap between monopsony and competitive employment is already specified, so the marginal social-gain explanation requires no figure.
graph_findings.repair: Leave both employment outcomes and the supply/MRP comparison to the graph; require a graph-specific employment interval together with the explanation that wages are transfers and forgone mutually beneficial hires reduce surplus.

graph_findings.construct: Specific versus general results of simultaneous labor-demand and supply shifts
graph_findings.why: Only the key permits offsetting wage effects or distinguishes an unchanged wage in this case from a universal rule. The other choices deny simultaneous shifts, fix employment by law, or contradict derived demand.
graph_findings.repair: Keep at least two theoretically possible final wages/employment changes, distinguished by the intersections; retain an incorrect claim that the actual offset must occur in every case.

graph_findings.construct: Lorenz shares, relative versus absolute income, Gini interpretation and proportional invariance
graph_findings.why: The question either asks a general definition/limitation of Lorenz curves and Gini, supplies the lower-Gini direction, or states every income share and total needed for the calculation.
graph_findings.repair: Require a particular curve or cumulative share to be read, then retain the inequality, group-mean, proportional-invariance or relative-versus-absolute interpretation. Use two plausible share calculations and an actual-value option with the wrong economic inference.

graph_findings.construct: Cumulative income shares versus population shares and Lorenz dominance
graph_findings.why: Only the key distinguishes population from income correctly, or explains Gini ordering through one Lorenz curve lying entirely below another. The other explanations confuse dollars and percentages, reverse the complement, or use irrelevant endpoints/means.
graph_findings.repair: Keep two valid income-share calculations at different readings, or two named curve orderings with coherent Gini implications; retain the actual reading paired with the relevant misconception.

graph_findings.construct: Gains from exchange measured as total surplus
graph_findings.why: Both full demand and supply equations are given. Their intersection and the total-surplus area follow without the graph.
graph_findings.repair: Obtain an intercept or equilibrium from the figure and retain interpretation of gains above resource cost; avoid merely asking for the coordinates.

graph_findings.construct: Distribution of gains from trade and positive net national surplus
graph_findings.why: Only the key has welfare components that sum consistently and a positive net gain from opening a standard small-country market. The others claim losses or unchanged total surplus despite stated gains exceeding losses.
graph_findings.repair: Offer two arithmetically consistent, economically possible trade/welfare packages with different graph-derived quantities and areas, plus the correct magnitudes with a reversed distributional interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Private versus social incentives, optimal correction, social marginal equality and public-good underprovision
graph_findings.why: The stem asks the definition of an externality correction/efficient outcome, supplies the corrective direction or full versus partial correction, or gives both private and social provision levels. The textbook principle selects the key without any plotted evidence.
graph_findings.repair: Require the particular private/social intersection, residual marginal gap or benefit comparison from the graph, together with the reason the policy corrects or fails to correct incentives. Preserve the distinction between social gains and transfers.

graph_findings.construct: Corrective-policy calibration, welfare gains, public-good provision and marginal decision rules
graph_findings.why: Only the keyed alternative consistently applies marginal social benefit/cost and treats transfers separately from real costs. Alternatives assume any policy size works, a cap forces expansion, positive total benefit guarantees efficiency, terminal MC applies to every added unit, or transfers are resource gains/losses. The numerical content can be skipped.
graph_findings.repair: Retain at least two economically coherent policies/net-gain calculations with different graph-based marginal gaps, quantities or areas. Include the actual graph values attached to the targeted interpretation error, so both graph evidence and economics remain necessary.

graph_findings.construct: Tax revenue equals the tax per unit times taxed transactions
graph_findings.why: Both the $2 tax and 160-thousand quantity are in the stem; multiplication gives the key.
graph_findings.repair: Require reading the taxed quantity from the figure and applying the per-unit-tax times post-tax-transactions rule. Offer two plausible readings with that rule and the actual readings under a wrong tax-revenue calculation.

graph_findings.construct: Buyer price and seller receipt under a subsidy
graph_findings.why: The task explicitly asks for the policy wedge. Only B has buyers paying less than sellers receive; the other choices reverse the subsidy or remove its wedge.
graph_findings.repair: Use two buyer/seller pairs with the correct subsidy direction and different plotted price levels, plus the observed pair with the wrong incidence interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Nonrival consumption and vertical summation of marginal benefits
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies the common public-good quantity, the fact that benefits are summed vertically, or the omitted group's positive marginal benefit. The general summation/nonrivalry principle resolves the question.
graph_findings.repair: Require one or both groups' benefit readings at a plotted quantity and retain the justification for summing benefits rather than quantities. Pair actual values with a wrong aggregation rule and provide two plausible correctly aggregated values.

graph_findings.construct: Efficient public-good provision using aggregate marginal benefits
graph_findings.why: Only the key sums both beneficiaries at a common quantity and compares the result with MC. Other choices substitute one group, add quantities, average valuations, or deny that an added beneficiary can affect the optimum.
graph_findings.repair: Include two correctly aggregated marginal-benefit or efficient-quantity candidates differing in graph readings; retain the actual readings under an incorrect single-group or horizontal-addition interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Monopolistic-competition pricing, entry, zero profit, excess capacity and efficiency
graph_findings.why: The item asks a general pricing/entry/zero-profit relationship, or explicitly supplies the long-run condition, inefficient scale or markup to be explained. The correct statement is true without any particular plotted values.
graph_findings.repair: Keep the specific economic principle, but require a graph-derived price/ATC/MC comparison, excess-capacity magnitude, or before/after demand position. Offer two plausible readings with the correct principle and a real reading with a wrong efficiency/profit inference.

graph_findings.construct: Markup versus profit, entry adjustment, productive/allocative inefficiency and policy tradeoffs
graph_findings.why: Only the key uses P versus MC for allocative efficiency, P versus ATC for profit, entry acting through incumbent demand, or the correct excess-capacity/variety distinction. Distractors deny these basic relationships, so the numerical readings or pictured outcome need not be verified.
graph_findings.repair: Provide two economically coherent combinations of plotted price, cost and output readings, and at least one actual-value combination with the targeted wrong interpretation. Preserve markup versus economic profit and the limits of the firm-level welfare diagram.

graph_findings.construct: Monopoly marginal revenue, profit maximization, natural monopoly and average-cost pricing
graph_findings.why: The stem asks why monopoly MR is below price, why moving beyond the maximizing quantity loses profit, what characterizes natural monopoly, or why fair-return pricing breaks even. The generic economic condition identifies the answer.
graph_findings.repair: Require the plotted MR/MC relationship or regulated price/ATC at a particular output and apply the same economic explanation. Do not state the optimizing or break-even conclusion before asking students to infer it.

graph_findings.construct: Monopoly output/pricing, fixed-cost effects, allocative losses and regulated cost recovery
graph_findings.why: Only the key respects the monopoly MR=MC/pricing rule, the direction of price and output along demand, unchanged marginal choices after fixed-cost changes, or the distinction between P=ATC and P=MC. Other numerical packages violate these rules or their own stated price/cost arithmetic.
graph_findings.repair: Use two theoretically consistent price/output/profit or subsidy packages with different readings from the graph. Keep a distractor with the actual graph values but the wrong profit, efficiency or financing interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Monopoly profit, marginal decisions, fixed costs, shutdown and lost gains from trade
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies the relevant price-cost condition or asks the general formula/rule: P versus ATC, MR below price, unchanged marginal conditions, AVC coverage, fixed cost after shutdown, or the meaning of restricting quantity below D=MC. No plotted evidence distinguishes the answer.
graph_findings.repair: Keep each item’s particular decision or explanation. Require a plotted price-cost comparison or an identified output interval, and pair that reading with the profit, shutdown, fixed-cost or forgone-gain inference. Use two viable readings with correct reasoning and a real reading with the targeted misconception.

graph_findings.construct: Monopoly deadweight loss versus a transfer
graph_findings.why: Only the deadweight-loss answer describes forgone mutually beneficial trades. The other choices equate the shaded region with all monopoly profit, tariff revenue or fixed cost.
graph_findings.repair: Offer competing plausible regions/endpoints for forgone trades, plus the actual region misidentified as a transfer; require comparing willingness to pay with marginal cost.

graph_findings.construct: Cartel profit maximization, competitive comparison or kinked-demand pricing
graph_findings.why: The stem provides the demand equations and marginal cost needed to solve the equilibrium algebraically; the attached figure contributes no missing evidence.
graph_findings.repair: Obtain a necessary demand intercept, slope or marginal-revenue boundary from the figure, then retain the cartel-versus-competitive or kinked-demand reasoning. Do not turn the task into reporting coordinates.

graph_findings.construct: Kinked-demand price rigidity and fixed-cost effects
graph_findings.why: The non-key options violate the stated cost arithmetic, make fixed cost alter marginal cost, or combine price and quantity changes inconsistent with the unchanged demand schedule. Students need not verify whether the new MC lies inside the plotted MR gap.
graph_findings.repair: Offer two coherent cost-change outcomes that differ in whether MC crosses the actual MR-gap boundary; retain the distinction between marginal and fixed costs and any requested profit calculation.

graph_findings.construct: Individual best responses versus joint-profit maximization
graph_findings.why: Only the key evaluates equilibrium through individual incentives. Other choices assert equilibrium from joint totals or one player’s payoff alone, or infer joint optimality from one player’s payoff.
graph_findings.repair: Use at least two credible sets of equilibrium cells and joint optima. Require checking unilateral deviations as well as joint totals, including an actual high-total cell incorrectly called an equilibrium.

graph_findings.construct: How a cell-specific payoff change affects Nash equilibria
graph_findings.why: The alternatives claim changing A/X removes the incentive at an unchanged B/Y cell, cannot alter any best response, or that unequal payoffs maximize joint payoff. Only the key gives a coherent strategic explanation.
graph_findings.repair: Give two plausible post-change equilibrium sets supported by rival unilateral-deviation calculations; include the actual joint maximum under a wrong stability inference.

graph_findings.construct: Profit per unit, total profit/loss and break-even
graph_findings.why: The task asks the general price-versus-ATC comparison, the profit/loss rectangle height, or what P minus ATC measures. These identities do not depend on the pictured levels.
graph_findings.repair: Require reading P and ATC at the economically appropriate output, then interpreting the result as per-unit profit/loss or break-even; preserve the distinction from AVC and total profit.

graph_findings.construct: Short-run operation versus shutdown, unavoidable fixed cost and policy incentives
graph_findings.why: The stem explicitly provides P relative to AVC/ATC, or says the subsidy crosses the shutdown threshold. The operating comparison follows without reading the graph.
graph_findings.repair: Read the current or policy-adjusted price against the plotted AVC threshold and ATC. Retain loss-minimization, unavoidable fixed cost and the distinction between lump-sum and per-unit incentives where present; do not announce the threshold crossing.

graph_findings.construct: Price taking and transmission from market to individual firm
graph_findings.why: The item asks the general rule linking market price to a firm’s horizontal MR, distinguishing market from firm quantity, or responding to a stated price increase with fixed costs. No particular coordinates are needed.
graph_findings.repair: Require the market equilibrium price and the firm’s rising-MC output from the two panels, then justify why market quantity is not the firm quantity and apply the price-taking decision.

graph_findings.construct: Entry/exit and market-to-firm long-run adjustment
graph_findings.why: The stem already announces profit, loss, entry, exit or the price direction. The standard entry/exit and rising-MC response answers the question without the figure.
graph_findings.repair: Require diagnosing profit/loss from plotted P and ATC and tracing the resulting supply/price/output change using pictured endpoints; preserve the short-run/long-run sequence.

graph_findings.construct: Zero economic profit and allocative versus productive efficiency
graph_findings.why: The stem labels the outcome long-run competitive equilibrium, states P=MC or minimum ATC, or states tangency. The requested zero-profit/efficiency conclusion is already implied.
graph_findings.repair: Require identifying the plotted P, MC, ATC and efficient-scale relationship, then distinguish zero profit from allocative and productive efficiency; include a real reading paired with the wrong efficiency interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Constant-, increasing- and decreasing-cost industry supply
graph_findings.why: The stem names the industry type or curve slope and asks its standard cost/price implication.
graph_findings.repair: Require inferring the type from two plotted long-run equilibria, and explain the associated change in input costs or firms’ minimum LRAC. Keep graph-specific evidence and the industry-cost explanation together.

graph_findings.construct: Profit-maximizing output and marginal versus fixed-cost effects
graph_findings.why: The question asks the generic order of analysis/rising-MC rule or states that an unavoidable fee exceeds profit without changing marginal costs. The graph supplies no necessary missing condition.
graph_findings.repair: Retain the marginal decision rule but require a labeled crossing or plotted profit amount needed to evaluate the fee; compare operating profit/loss with shutdown and later exit where relevant.

graph_findings.construct: Competitive short-run supply and the shutdown threshold
graph_findings.why: The item asks the general MC-above-AVC supply definition, why MC below AVC is excluded, or fixed-versus-variable-cost effects.
graph_findings.repair: Require identifying a displayed eligible MC segment or deriving the old/new threshold from plotted AVC, then explain the supply or cost-shift implication.

graph_findings.construct: Profit maximization, economic versus accounting profit, loss minimization and exit
graph_findings.why: Only the key uses MR=MC and the correct P/ATC/AVC distinction. Other options select minimum ATC regardless of price, treat P>AVC as profit, erase fixed costs at shutdown, let a price taker set price, or reverse entry/exit. The displayed result need not be checked.
graph_findings.repair: Offer two plausible operating/profit outcomes differing in plotted cost or output readings. Include actual readings with a wrong shutdown/profit interpretation, and preserve any long-run exit inference.

graph_findings.construct: Short-run supply and shutdown boundary
graph_findings.why: Only the key applies rising MC above minimum AVC or indifference at the shutdown point. Alternatives use all MC, ATC, zero costs, permanent output or price setting.
graph_findings.repair: Provide two feasible labeled threshold/output candidates consistent with the general supply rule, then require the graph’s AVC and MC relationship to select and economically justify the result.

graph_findings.construct: Fixed-cost independence of the shutdown price
graph_findings.why: Only the unchanged-price option respects the stated unchanged MC and AVC; its $20 value need not be read.
graph_findings.repair: Give two unchanged-threshold amounts and two changed-threshold interpretations, forcing both a graph reading and recognition that fixed cost does not set shutdown.

graph_findings.construct: Market-to-firm transmission, profit and competitive adjustment
graph_findings.why: Only the key treats the market price as firm MR and applies rising MC; the alternatives make the firm set market price, confuse aggregate and firm quantity, shift MC solely from demand, or imply shutdown at ATC.
graph_findings.repair: Use two internally consistent market-price/firm-output sequences with different graph readings, plus the actual values interpreted using the wrong price-taking or entry rule.

graph_findings.construct: Limits of inferring firm counts from paired market/firm panels
graph_findings.why: Only the key recognizes missing information about identical outputs and units; the other choices call firm quantity a price, deny measurable market quantity or deny equilibrium.
graph_findings.repair: Make the alternatives depend on the actual axis scales and whether the pictured representative firm is sufficient evidence of identical outputs. Keep the inference limit rather than simply dividing two coordinates.

graph_findings.construct: Competitive long-run equilibrium conditions
graph_findings.why: Only P=MC=minimum ATC is a coherent operating long-run equilibrium; other pairs include negative fixed cost, shutdown or positive profit with MC below AVC.
graph_findings.repair: Offer two coherent plotted price-cost/output relationships and distinguish the equilibrium/efficiency implications of each.

graph_findings.construct: Marginal efficiency of competitive equilibrium
graph_findings.why: The stem identifies E as an efficient competitive equilibrium; marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost is the general explanation.
graph_findings.repair: Require a marginal benefit/cost comparison at E and a nearby plotted quantity, retaining why additional or forgone trades change total surplus.

graph_findings.construct: Consumer surplus versus expenditure; transfers versus total surplus
graph_findings.why: The stem gives the intercept, equilibrium quantity and price needed to calculate the surplus, and any transfer amount. The graph repeats the supplied data.
graph_findings.repair: Read one necessary intercept or price from the figure and retain the expenditure-versus-surplus or redistribution-versus-efficiency diagnosis.

graph_findings.construct: Long-run monopolistic competition, entry and the profit-maximizing stopping rule
graph_findings.why: Tangency at the long-run output, an outward demand shift with fixed costs, or expanding beyond the selected MR=MC quantity gives the theoretical answer without particular plotted evidence.
graph_findings.repair: Require plotted P/ATC/MC or MR/MC comparisons at the candidate output, then retain the markup, excess-capacity, entry or marginal-profit explanation.

graph_findings.construct: Corrective taxes and economic incidence
graph_findings.why: Only the key is compatible with a positive tax wedge and sharing rather than equating remittance with burden. Other choices reverse the wedge, give zero wedge, or assign all burden solely by statutory payment.
graph_findings.repair: Use two plausible buyer/seller price pairs with the same positive wedge but different burden splits; retain the legal-versus-economic incidence interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Tax effects on buyer/seller prices and quantity
graph_findings.why: Only the key lowers traded quantity while raising buyer price and/or lowering seller receipts. Alternatives reverse a basic tax effect or assert unchanged quantity for a reason unrelated to the pictured curves.
graph_findings.repair: Keep two plausible tax-induced price/quantity movements, differing in actual plotted magnitudes, and require explaining the wedge’s contraction of mutually beneficial trade.

graph_findings.construct: Tax wedge and supply-side tax representation
graph_findings.why: The task asks a generic tax consequence or what supply-plus-tax means. The general tax rule suffices.
graph_findings.repair: Require a graph-specific old/new quantity or vertical wedge, together with the tax-induced marginal incentive explanation.

graph_findings.construct: Tax revenue uses the full wedge and the post-tax quantity
graph_findings.why: Only the key uses both buyer/seller price changes and the appropriate post-tax quantity or quantity response. Other alternatives explicitly retain the original quantity, use buyer burden as the tax, or contain inconsistent stated revenue arithmetic.
graph_findings.repair: Give two internally coherent full-wedge/post-tax-quantity calculations that differ in graph readings; keep actual readings with an incorrect revenue-base or incidence interpretation.

graph_findings.construct: Tax revenue from the per-unit wedge and units traded
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies buyer price $18, seller receipt $12 and post-tax quantity 80, so revenue is calculable with no figure.
graph_findings.repair: Obtain at least one necessary price or quantity from the figure and retain distinguishing the total tax wedge from one side’s burden.

graph_findings.construct: Marginal versus average product at the MP–AP crossing
graph_findings.why: Only the key allows AP to change from rising to falling at the crossing. The alternatives have AP falling on both sides, rising on both sides, or zero on both sides; none can describe the stated crossing in the ordinary smooth production model. The missing alternative is a minimum, which would require inspecting crossing direction.
graph_findings.repair: Offer both an AP maximum and an AP minimum, each paired with a plausible observed ordering on either side of the marked labor input. Require that ordering from the figure and the marginal-average explanation.

graph_findings.construct: Close substitutes, elasticity and the total-revenue test
graph_findings.why: Only B consistently links more close substitutes to greater demand responsiveness and a revenue increase after a price cut in the elastic market. A and C mismatch those relationships; D equates an equal absolute price change with identical elasticity. The curve readings do not discriminate.
graph_findings.repair: Give two alternatives with the same correct substitute/elasticity/revenue relationship but different graph-derived interval elasticities or revenue totals. Retain the actual readings with a mistaken slope-versus-elasticity explanation.

graph_findings.construct: Relative inequality versus average living standards
graph_findings.why: The stem supplies both Gini values (0.380 and 0.252) and both mean incomes ($20,000 and $18,000). The 0.128 Gini decrease, 10% mean-income decline and limit on group-welfare inference follow without the Lorenz figure.
graph_findings.repair: Require the before/after income-share evidence from the plotted curves and combine it with the given mean incomes. Keep the distinction between a more equal distribution and higher absolute income; offer actual shares with the incorrect welfare inference.

graph_findings.construct: Nonbinding wage floor, shortage versus surplus, and distinguishing a floor from a ceiling
graph_findings.why: A is the only internally coherent policy diagnosis. B combines a binding floor and excess supply with a binding ceiling; C calls excess supply consistent with a binding floor at a price it also says is below equilibrium; D combines a binding floor with excess demand. The $12 equilibrium and 200-thousand employment/gap values need never be checked.
graph_findings.repair: Keep the existing multi-error diagnosis and opposite-control comparison. Offer two coherent nonbinding-floor/binding-ceiling diagnoses with different graph-derived equilibrium or gap values, plus the actual values under the wrong control interpretation.
graph_findings.prior_work_check: Absent from the 126 General wording/graph changes and the 38 construct-drift closure changes. This is a concrete residual distractor shortcut, not a request to revisit its approved difficulty or multi-error construct.

graph_findings.construct: Movement along supply versus a shift of supply
graph_findings.why: A says any quantity increase is an increase in supply; B calls the claimed positive supply change a leftward shift; C treats a higher quantity alone as proof of a demand shift. Only D gives the movement-versus-shift correction. The specific A/B positions and 125-thousand amount are unused.
graph_findings.repair: Retain the misconception diagnosis and require the actual starting/ending price and quantity or a graph-specific magnitude. Include two correctly interpreted movements with different plotted values and the actual values mislabeled as a supply shift.
graph_findings.prior_work_check: Absent from the 126 General wording/graph changes and the 38 construct-drift closure changes. Preserve its approved current difficulty; only the unaddressed choice-elimination route is flagged.

calibration_examples.why_it_works: The graph supplies the price changes and lost-trade surplus, giving $9 lost CS but only $8 of tax burden on continuing trades. A and D both describe a loss larger than the $8 burden; theory alone cannot choose the amount. Reading prices alone is also insufficient: students must distinguish the transfer from forgone surplus.

The figure supplies the AC–AVC separation at Q=50. Students must use that difference to infer fixed cost, then spread the same fixed cost over Q=25, giving AFC=$16. The cost identity and fixed-versus-average distinction are essential; the requested AFC is not simply a displayed coordinate.

C and B supply the midpoint inputs. Choices C and D are both theoretically coherent revenue/elasticity pairs, so the graph is needed to choose 1.67/elastic rather than 1.00/unit elastic. The calculation must then be interpreted with the total-revenue test.

The actual short-run and long-run endpoints determine elasticities of about 0.23 and 0.75 and whether 90 units can be supplied at $8. B and C agree on the ordinary time-horizon rule and elasticities but disagree on procurement feasibility. Graph evidence and the distinction between responsiveness and available quantity both matter.

Payoffs must be read to check each firm’s best responses and to compare joint profits. A and D both posit the same Nash equilibrium but name different joint maxima. The key is B/Y with total 11 versus A/X with total 18; maximizing joint profit alone does not identify a Nash equilibrium.

The figure is needed to select Q=30 and distinguish a $300 profit from a $300 loss. A and D are both possible operating cases before the figure is seen. Students still must apply MR=MC, compare P with ATC for profit, and check AVC for short-run operation.

40032.stem: Refer to the graph. A student says a $6 minimum wage binds, fixes employment at 300 thousand and creates a 200-thousand-worker surplus. Which diagnosis corrects the claim and identifies the policy that could sustain the gap at $6?

choices.A: Nonbinding floor: $12 and 200 thousand; at $6, Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage ceiling.
choices.B: Binding floor: $6 and 300 thousand; Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage ceiling.
choices.C: Nonbinding floor: $12 and 200 thousand; at $6, Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage floor.
choices.D: Binding floor: $6 and 100 thousand; Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage floor.

40032.correct_answer: Nonbinding floor: $12 and 200 thousand; at $6, Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage ceiling.
40032.feedback: The $6 minimum is below the $12 equilibrium, so wage and employment remain $12 and 200 thousand. At a hypothetical $6 wage, firms demand 300 thousand workers but only 100 thousand offer labor: a shortage, not surplus. A binding wage ceiling could prevent wage from rising; the floor does not.

40040.stem: Refer to the graph. Which complete pre/post comparison is correct?

choices.A: Buyer price +2, seller price -2, quantity -50 thousand
choices.B: Buyer price +4, seller price unchanged, quantity +50 thousand
choices.C: Buyer price +4, seller price -4, quantity unchanged
choices.D: Buyer price -2, seller price +2, quantity -50 thousand

40040.correct_answer: Buyer price +2, seller price -2, quantity -50 thousand
40040.feedback: The market moves from price 12, quantity 250 to buyer 14, seller 10, quantity 200.

40041.stem: Refer to the rideshare graph with A at quantity 250 thousand. A proposal halves the displayed per-trip tax. Keeping the straight demand and supply curves fixed, what happens to daily tax revenue?

choices.A: It falls from $800,000 to $400,000 because quantity stays fixed
choices.B: It falls from $800,000 to $450,000 as quantity rises to 225,000
choices.C: It rises from $800,000 to $900,000 as quantity rises to 225,000
choices.D: It falls from $1,000,000 to $500,000 using the untaxed quantity

40041.correct_answer: It falls from $800,000 to $450,000 as quantity rises to 225,000
40041.feedback: The displayed wedge is $14 − $10 = $4 at 200,000 trips. Halving it to $2 places quantity halfway between 200,000 and the untaxed 250,000: 225,000. Revenue changes from $4 × 200,000 = $800,000 to $2 × 225,000 = $450,000. The quantity response offsets part of the rate cut.

42023.stem: Based on the graph, why does the unregulated fast-fashion garments outcome differ from the socially efficient outcome?

choices.A: The efficient outcome ignores all external effects
choices.B: The market outcome already includes the full spillover
choices.C: The difference is caused only by statutory tax incidence
choices.D: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve

42023.correct_answer: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve
42023.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 240 million garments and $12. By contrast, the socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 160 million garments and $15. The social outcome includes the spillover that private choices omit.

42028.stem: Based on the fast-fashion garments graph, which corrective-policy claim is economically accurate?

choices.A: a $6 corrective tax per garment would close the marginal private-social gap
choices.B: Any $1 policy would necessarily restore efficiency
choices.C: The policy should move quantity farther from the social outcome
choices.D: The policy amount should equal market price rather than the spillover

42028.correct_answer: a $6 corrective tax per garment would close the marginal private-social gap
42028.feedback: The tax makes producers face the $6 marginal external cost, aligning private marginal cost with MSC and moving quantity to 160 million garments. The optimal per-unit correction equals the marginal external effect, $6 per garment.

42033.stem: Based on the graph, why does the unregulated disposable vapes outcome differ from the socially efficient outcome?

choices.A: The efficient outcome ignores all external effects
choices.B: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve
choices.C: The market outcome already includes the full spillover
choices.D: The difference is caused only by statutory tax incidence

42033.correct_answer: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve
42033.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 180 thousand vapes and $10. By contrast, the socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 140 thousand vapes and $8. The social outcome includes the spillover that private choices omit.

42038.stem: Based on the disposable vapes graph, which corrective-policy claim is economically accurate?

choices.A: Any $1 policy would necessarily restore efficiency
choices.B: The policy should move quantity farther from the social outcome
choices.C: a $4 corrective tax per vape would close the marginal private-social gap
choices.D: The policy amount should equal market price rather than the spillover

42038.correct_answer: a $4 corrective tax per vape would close the marginal private-social gap
42038.feedback: The tax makes consumers face the $4 marginal external cost, aligning their private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 140 thousand vapes. The optimal per-unit correction equals the marginal external effect, $4 per vape.

42043.stem: Based on the graph, why does the unregulated native-plant gardens outcome differ from the socially efficient outcome?

choices.A: The efficient outcome ignores all external effects
choices.B: The market outcome already includes the full spillover
choices.C: The difference is caused only by statutory tax incidence
choices.D: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve

42043.correct_answer: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve
42043.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 100 gardens and $12. By contrast, the socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 150 gardens and $10. The social outcome includes the spillover that private choices omit.

42047.stem: Refer to the native-plant gardens graph. A council proposes only an upper cap of 150 gardens, with no subsidy or purchase commitment. Starting from the private market outcome, which assessment is correct?

choices.A: The cap forces output to rise to 150 gardens without changing incentives.
choices.B: The cap cuts output to 50 gardens because 150 is the reduction target.
choices.C: The cap produces 150 gardens by making producers receive the full external benefit.
choices.D: The cap is nonbinding at 100 gardens; an incentive to expand is still needed.

42047.correct_answer: The cap is nonbinding at 100 gardens; an incentive to expand is still needed.
42047.feedback: The private intersection is 100 gardens; the social intersection is 150. A maximum of 150 permits the existing 100 and gives no incentive to supply the extra gardens. A subsidy or appropriately designed provision commitment can support expansion.

42048.stem: Based on the native-plant gardens graph, which corrective-policy claim is economically accurate?

choices.A: a $5 producer subsidy per garden would close the marginal private-social gap
choices.B: Any $1 policy would necessarily restore efficiency
choices.C: The policy should move quantity farther from the social outcome
choices.D: The policy amount should equal market price rather than the spillover

42048.correct_answer: a $5 producer subsidy per garden would close the marginal private-social gap
42048.feedback: The producer subsidy rewards the $5 marginal external benefit, aligning the producer's effective cost with MSC and moving quantity to 150 gardens. The optimal per-unit correction equals the marginal external effect, $5 per garden.

42053.stem: Based on the graph, why does the unregulated public-transit rides outcome differ from the socially efficient outcome?

choices.A: The efficient outcome ignores all external effects
choices.B: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve
choices.C: The market outcome already includes the full spillover
choices.D: The difference is caused only by statutory tax incidence

42053.correct_answer: The market uses private incentives, while efficiency uses the relevant social marginal curve
42053.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 150 thousand rides per day and $5. By contrast, the socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 200 thousand rides per day and $6. The social outcome includes the spillover that private choices omit.

42057.stem: Refer to the public-transit rides graph. A transport authority wants the social-intersection quantity. Which proposal directly supports that target rather than merely allowing it?

choices.A: An upper cap of 200 thousand rides with fares and private incentives unchanged.
choices.B: A $2 rider subsidy that raises the private incentive and supports 200 thousand rides per day.
choices.C: A $2 tax on riders that lowers their private incentive to travel.
choices.D: A requirement to keep private provision at 150 thousand rides per day.

42057.correct_answer: A $2 rider subsidy that raises the private incentive and supports 200 thousand rides per day.
42057.feedback: MSB intersects MPC at 200 thousand rides; private demand supports 150 thousand. The $2 external benefit can be internalized with a rider subsidy. A nonbinding maximum does not induce additional trips.

42058.stem: Based on the public-transit rides graph, which corrective-policy claim is economically accurate?

choices.A: Any $1 policy would necessarily restore efficiency
choices.B: The policy should move quantity farther from the social outcome
choices.C: a $2 rider subsidy per ride would close the marginal private-social gap
choices.D: The policy amount should equal market price rather than the spillover

42058.correct_answer: a $2 rider subsidy per ride would close the marginal private-social gap
42058.feedback: The rider subsidy rewards the $2 marginal external benefit, aligning the rider's private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 200 thousand rides per day. The optimal per-unit correction equals the marginal external effect, $2 per ride.

42062.stem: Which corrective instrument and per-unit amount shown on the graph would move fast-fashion garments to the efficient quantity?

choices.A: a $1 corrective tax per unit
choices.B: a $6 per garment policy in the opposite direction
choices.C: a $6 corrective tax per garment
choices.D: a quantity target at 240 million garments

42062.feedback: The tax makes producers face the $6 marginal external cost, aligning private marginal cost with MSC and moving quantity to 160 million garments. Therefore the graph's optimal instrument is a $6 corrective tax per garment.

42065.stem: Why does the corrected quantity of 160 million garments represent social efficiency in this market?

choices.A: Tax revenue or subsidy spending is maximized there
choices.B: Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost there
choices.C: Buyers and sellers receive equal dollar gains there
choices.D: Private curves remain at their original market intersection there

42065.correct_answer: Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost there
42065.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 160 million garments and $15. At that intersection, marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, so no additional mutually beneficial unit is omitted and no inefficient unit is produced.

42066.stem: Refer to the garments graph. Suppose the $6 corrective tax is legally remitted by sellers. Relative to the unregulated price, which result separates statutory payment from economic burden?

choices.A: Buyers pay $6 more and sellers receive the original $12 because sellers remit the tax.
choices.B: Sellers receive $6 less and buyers keep paying $12 because sellers remit the tax.
choices.C: Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less per garment; legal remittance does not assign the whole burden.
choices.D: Both sides still face $12 because the tax changes only government receipts.

42066.correct_answer: Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less per garment; legal remittance does not assign the whole burden.
42066.feedback: The original price is $12. At Q = 160 million, buyers pay $15 and sellers receive $9: a $3 change on each side and a $6 wedge. The burden follows equilibrium price changes, not who sends the payment.

42067.stem: How does the corrective tax change private incentives in the fast-fashion garments market?

choices.A: It removes scarcity from the market
choices.B: It guarantees equal surplus for buyers and sellers
choices.C: It preserves market quantity while changing only transfers
choices.D: It makes the private decision-maker face the marginal social effect

42067.correct_answer: It makes the private decision-maker face the marginal social effect
42067.feedback: The tax makes producers face the $6 marginal external cost, aligning private marginal cost with MSC and moving quantity to 160 million garments. Internalization changes the marginal choice; it does not remove scarcity or guarantee equal gains.

42068.stem: Which conclusion is inconsistent with the correctly calibrated fast-fashion garments policy shown on the graph?

choices.A: Any policy with the correct direction automatically has the optimal size
choices.B: The optimal wedge equals the marginal external effect
choices.C: Corrected quantity equates social marginal benefit and cost
choices.D: Policy can create a price difference between buyers and sellers

42068.correct_answer: Any policy with the correct direction automatically has the optimal size
42068.feedback: A policy must have both the correct direction and the correct size. Here the optimal wedge equals $6 per garment; a smaller or larger intervention would leave a quantity distortion.

42071.stem: Which corrective instrument and per-unit amount shown on the graph would move disposable vapes to the efficient quantity?

choices.A: a $1 corrective tax per unit
choices.B: a $4 per vape policy in the opposite direction
choices.C: a quantity target at 180 thousand vapes
choices.D: a $4 corrective tax per vape

42071.feedback: The tax makes consumers face the $4 marginal external cost, aligning their private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 140 thousand vapes. Therefore the graph's optimal instrument is a $4 corrective tax per vape.

42074.stem: Why does the corrected quantity of 140 thousand vapes represent social efficiency in this market?

choices.A: Tax revenue or subsidy spending is maximized there
choices.B: Buyers and sellers receive equal dollar gains there
choices.C: Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost there
choices.D: Private curves remain at their original market intersection there

42074.correct_answer: Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost there
42074.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MPC intersects MSB, at 140 thousand vapes and $8. At that intersection, marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, so no additional mutually beneficial unit is omitted and no inefficient unit is produced.

42075.stem: At the corrected disposable vapes quantity, which buyer-price and seller-receipt pair reflects the policy wedge?

choices.A: Buyers pay $8; sellers receive $12
choices.B: Both sides face $10
choices.C: Both sides face $8
choices.D: Buyers pay $12; sellers receive $8

42075.feedback: At 140 thousand vapes, buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $8. The $4 per vape difference is the corrective tax wedge, not deadweight loss.

42076.stem: How does the corrective tax change private incentives in the disposable vapes market?

choices.A: It makes the private decision-maker face the marginal social effect
choices.B: It removes scarcity from the market
choices.C: It guarantees equal surplus for buyers and sellers
choices.D: It preserves market quantity while changing only transfers

42076.correct_answer: It makes the private decision-maker face the marginal social effect
42076.feedback: The tax makes consumers face the $4 marginal external cost, aligning their private incentive with MSB and moving quantity to 140 thousand vapes. Internalization changes the marginal choice; it does not remove scarcity or guarantee equal gains.

42077.stem: Which conclusion is inconsistent with the correctly calibrated disposable vapes policy shown on the graph?

choices.A: The optimal wedge equals the marginal external effect
choices.B: Any policy with the correct direction automatically has the optimal size
choices.C: Corrected quantity equates social marginal benefit and cost
choices.D: Policy can create a price difference between buyers and sellers

42077.correct_answer: Any policy with the correct direction automatically has the optimal size
42077.feedback: A policy must have both the correct direction and the correct size. Here the optimal wedge equals $4 per vape; a smaller or larger intervention would leave a quantity distortion.

42080.stem: Which corrective instrument and per-unit amount shown on the graph would move native-plant gardens to the efficient quantity?

choices.A: a $5 producer subsidy per garden
choices.B: a $1 producer subsidy per unit
choices.C: a $5 per garden policy in the opposite direction
choices.D: a quantity target at 100 gardens

42080.feedback: The producer subsidy rewards the $5 marginal external benefit, aligning the producer's effective cost with MSC and moving quantity to 150 gardens. Therefore the graph's optimal instrument is a $5 producer subsidy per garden.

42083.stem: Why does the corrected quantity of 150 gardens represent social efficiency in this market?

choices.A: Tax revenue or subsidy spending is maximized there
choices.B: Buyers and sellers receive equal dollar gains there
choices.C: Private curves remain at their original market intersection there
choices.D: Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost there

42083.correct_answer: Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost there
42083.feedback: The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 150 gardens and $10. At that intersection, marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, so no additional mutually beneficial unit is omitted and no inefficient unit is produced.

42084.stem: Refer to the gardens graph. A producer subsidy supports the social-intersection quantity. Which fiscal and price account is consistent with both the graph and payment on every garden produced?

choices.A: Buyers pay $10, sellers receive $15, and the subsidy budget is $750.
choices.B: Buyers pay $15, sellers receive $10, and tax revenue is $750.
choices.C: Buyers pay $10, sellers receive $15, and the subsidy budget is $250.
choices.D: Buyers pay $12, sellers receive $17, and the subsidy budget is $500.

42084.correct_answer: Buyers pay $10, sellers receive $15, and the subsidy budget is $750.
42084.feedback: At 150 gardens, MPB is $10 and MPC is $15. A $5 subsidy bridges them, so total expenditure is 5 x 150 = $750; paying only for the 50 additional gardens is a different program.

42085.stem: How does the producer subsidy change private incentives in the native-plant gardens market?

choices.A: It removes scarcity from the market
choices.B: It makes the private decision-maker face the marginal social effect
choices.C: It guarantees equal surplus for buyers and sellers
choices.D: It preserves market quantity while changing only transfers

42085.correct_answer: It makes the private decision-maker face the marginal social effect
42085.feedback: The producer subsidy rewards the $5 marginal external benefit, aligning the producer's effective cost with MSC and moving quantity to 150 gardens. Internalization changes the marginal choice; it does not remove scarcity or guarantee equal gains.
